title: Lesson 70: Reliability Engineering: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets, and Runbooks for Agent Operations
description: The reliability-engineering toolkit: SLIs that measure user experience, SLOs that contract it, error budgets that decide when a bad week stops releases, and runbooks that tell a calm stranger what to do.

questions.question: Per the lesson, an architect sets a solution SLO at 99.5% while the platform SLA is 99.9%. Why is staying below the platform number the right call?
options: Because a solution SLO must always be more stringent than the platform SLA to protect users.
Because matching the platform SLA leaves no error budget for application-layer failures, integration issues, or planned maintenance in the same measurement window.
Because the platform SLA is a hard cap that a solution SLO can never exceed.
Because 99.5% is the highest availability any Salesforce solution can realistically achieve.
questions.explanation: If the platform SLA and the solution SLO are both 99.9%, any significant platform downtime consumes the entire error budget, leaving no buffer for the failure classes the architect owns.

questions.question: An agent service processes 200,000 runs in a month against a 99.8% availability SLO. What is the monthly error budget in failed runs?
questions.explanation: The error budget is 100% minus the SLO, so 0.2%. 200,000 times 0.2% equals 400 failed runs allowed per month.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on SLIs for a system that runs autonomous agents?
options: Availability is the only SLI that matters, because an agent that completes a run has succeeded.
An agent can finish without error and still be wrong, so quality SLIs such as acceptance rate or hallucination rate belong in the suite alongside availability and latency.
User-caused errors should count against a success-rate SLO because they still render an error to the user.
SLIs should be set per technical component so each box in the architecture has its own target.
questions.explanation: Agent completion is not proof of correctness, so quality SLIs are required; only system-caused errors count against success-rate SLOs, and SLOs are set per business capability, not per component.
